content: Sucralfate is an antiulcer agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of active duodenal ulcers. It is typically administered orally at a dose of 1 gram (10 mL or 2 teaspoons) four times daily on an empty stomach. Antacids may be used for pain relief but should not be taken within 30 minutes before or after sucralfate administration. While healing may occur within the first one to two weeks of treatment, therapy should continue for 4 to 8 weeks unless healing is confirmed by X-ray or endoscopic examination. In elderly patients, dosing should be approached cautiously, starting at the lower end of the dosing range due to the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of other diseases or concurrent drug therapies. Off-label uses of sucralfate include topical application for burn patients to reduce healing time, combination therapy with ranitidine for ulcer management, and rectal retention enemas for specific conditions. Pediatric use is limited, with insufficient data on FDA-labeled or off-label applications. Sucralfate is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the active substance or its excipients. Episodes of hyperglycemia have been reported in diabetic patients, necessitating close monitoring of blood glucose levels and potential adjustments to antidiabetic medications. Patients with chronic renal failure or those on dialysis should use sucralfate cautiously due to the risk of aluminum accumulation and toxicity, as small amounts of aluminum are absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract during sucralfate administration. Drug interactions have been observed with sucralfate, reducing the bioavailability of medications such as cimetidine, digoxin, fluoroquinolone antibiotics, ketoconazole, L-thyroxine, phenytoin, quinidine, ranitidine, tetracycline, and theophylline. To avoid these interactions, concomitant medications should be administered at least two hours before sucralfate. Monitoring is recommended when bioavailability alterations are critical. Adverse reactions to sucralfate are generally mild, with constipation being the most common complaint. Other reported side effects include gastrointestinal discomfort, dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, rash, and back pain. Post-marketing reports have noted hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, lip swelling, and respiratory tract edema. Bezoars have been reported in patients with delayed gastric emptying or those receiving enteral tube feedings. Sucralfate is minimally absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, and acute overdose risks are low. Symptoms of overdose, when present, include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Chronic overdose data is limited, and no specific treatment recommendations are available. The mechanism of action of sucralfate involves forming an ulcer-adherent complex at the ulcer site, providing a protective barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile salts. It also inhibits pepsin activity and adsorbs bile salts. Sucralfate is primarily excreted in the urine. Sucralfate suspension contains 1 gram of sucralfate per 10 mL and includes excipients such as colloidal silicon dioxide, glycerin, methylcellulose, and simethicone. It should be stored at controlled room temperature (20-25°C or 68-77°F) and shaken well before use. Freezing should be avoided. In pregnancy, sucralfate is classified as Category B by the FDA, with no evidence of harm to the fetus in animal studies. However, it should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, as adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. Its excretion in human milk is unknown, so caution is advised when administering to nursing mothers. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established, and geriatric patients should be monitored for renal function due to the risk of toxicity. Sucralfate is not intended for intravenous administration, as inadvertent injection has led to fatal complications, including pulmonary and cerebral emboli.
